How i found in Zoho CRMEvery Expert Has One Story They Never Forget. This Is Mine.
Every cybersecurity researcher remembers the vulnerability that changed the way they think. This is my story.

Before We begin, let’s take a look at my bio,
Hi My name is Muthu Kumar, My journey began with programming in 10th grade and evolved into a passion for cybersecurity. I realized building a system is an art, but securing it is a responsibility. I enjoy uncovering real-world vulnerabilities, thinking like an attacker, and helping organizations and strengthen their Security.
People often ask me:
- What do you do?
- Why did you choose cybersecurity?
- How do you find vulnerabilities?
My simple answer is,
I don't start by looking for vulnerabilities.
I start by understanding the Hows application works.
Because...
"You can’t break something until you understand how it works.”
---
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Its a one of Leading product in Zoho CorporationWhy I Chose Zoho CRM
I selected Zoho CRM because it is one of Zoho's biggest and most widely used products. Thousands of businesses rely on it every day.
Instead of running automated scanners immediately, I decided to become a normal user.
I explored every feature manually like created customers & added contacts, created tasks,scheduled meetings, explored deals, tested calls, uploaded documents.
I visited every page I could find.
For hours, I simply learned how the application behaved.
"Curiosity finds more bugs than automation."
---
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Vulnerable FeatureThe Small Features That Changed Everything,
While exploring, I noticed an interesting feature.
Users could attach a URL instead of uploading a file.
It looked completely normal.
But something felt unusual.
Whenever I feel that curiosity, I stop and investigate.
I opened Burp Suite and captured the request.
Then I carefully studied:
- Request parameters
- Response
- Headers
- API endpoint
Endpoint of the productEverything looked normal.
Next, I sent the request to Repeater.
The first replay worked exactly as expected.
Then I asked myself...
"What happens if I replace the attachment URL with my own server?"
So I replaced the URL parameter with my Interactsh callback URL.
I clicked Send.
The server responded:
200 OK
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Successfully send request 200 okAt first, nothing appeared unusual.
Then I checked Interactsh...
A few seconds later...
DNS interaction received.
Then...
HTTP interaction received.
The requests originated from Zoho's infrastructure.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Successfully Got Interaction from ZohoAt that moment, I knew something important.
The server was making requests to my external server.
I had discovered a Blind Outbound SSRF.
Because the application never returned the fetched content, only the outbound interaction was visible.
That is why I classified it as a Blind SSRF.
---
The Best Feeling
I documented everything carefully.
I included:
- Steps to reproduce
- Burp requests
- Proof of Concept
- Interactsh evidence
- Impact analysis
Then I submitted the report.
The next day...
I opened my email.
The security team had updated my report.
They changed both the title and the severity.
I was incredibly happy.
I thought...
"This is it. My report has been accepted!"
It was one of the happiest moments of my bug bounty journey.
---
Then Reality Hit
The following day, another email arrived.
It said:
Unfortunately, this report is a duplicate. Another researcher reported it earlier.
For two days...
I couldn't stop thinking about it.
I barely slept.
I kept asking myself:
"What if I had found it one day earlier?"
It was painful.
But after some time, I realized something much more valuable.
Although I didn't receive a reward...
I had earned something nobody could take away.
It was painful 😣😭Experience.
---
This report taught me lotWhat This Report Really Taught Me
This report completely changed how I approach security research.
It taught me:
- Understand the application before attacking it.
- Small features often hide big vulnerabilities.
- Manual testing is powerful.
- Curiosity is your greatest tool.
- Every duplicate teaches you something new.
- Rejection is part of becoming a better researcher.
Today, I don't see that report as a failure.
I see it as the moment I started thinking like a real security researcher.
Duplicates don’t define your skills. Your persistence does.
Every rejected report is training for your next accepted one.
The best researchers are not the ones who never fail—they’re the ones who never stop looking.
---
My Message to Every Beginner
If your first report becomes a duplicate...
Don't quit.
If your report gets rejected...
Don't quit.
If someone finds it before you...
Don't quit.
Keep learning.
Keep exploring.
Keep asking questions.
Because one day...
Your next discovery could protect millions of users.
---
Thank You
Thank you for taking the time to read my journey.
How to you feel it guys Comment it..
If this story inspired you or reminded you of your own bug bounty experience, I would truly appreciate your support.
Feel free to like, share, or follow for more cybersecurity research, bug bounty stories, and lessons learned from real-world application security.
Happy Hunting!
